newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSIONER BACKS PM
Human rights commissioner, Chris Sidoti says he's encouraged by the Prime Minister's call for moderation, tolerance and sensitivity in the expression of free speech.
John Howard has told the Queensland Liberal Party convention that since coming to power, the Coaltion has lifted the pall of censorship in the Australian community.
Mr Howard claims that under Labor, people who expressed views which differed from the then government, they risked being labelled racist or bigoted.
He says he and Peter Reith were branded racists in a Melbourne Age cartoon last year for their views on the introduction of the Native Title Act.
Mr Sidoti has warned that John Howard's comments on free speech shouldn't be interpreted as a greenlight for intolerance.
FATE OF ASYLUM SEEKERS TO BE DECIDED
The fate of up to 13-hundred East Timorese asylum seekers in Australia is expected to be decided in a case going before the Federal Court today.
The test case on a citizenship issue follows a Federal Government decision last year that some asylum seekers have Portuguese citizenship.
The Christians in Solidarity with East Timor group intends to hold a vigil outside the court, to protest against what they see as Australia's bending to Indonesian government wishes.
NT CELEBRATES LAND RIGHTS IN NEW BOOK
A book detailing a warts-and-all picture of land rights in the Northern Territory has been commissioned by the Central Land Council.
The Council's Alex Wright is putting together the work which will celebrate 20 years of land rights in the Territory.
Ms Wright says the book will feature activists who fought hard to get land rights recognised, and provide a detailed picture of the Territory Land Rights Act.
She says it's hoped the book to be published next year, will help non-Aboriginal people understand the importance of land to indigenous people.
A.F.P CORRUPTION INQUIRY
The inquiry into allegations of corruption in Australia's Federal Police Force will today start approaching officers for questioning.
After its first week of deliberations the Harrison Inquiry has finalised its investigation team, which includes two Tasmanian police investigators appointed by the Commowealth Attorney General.
At this stage, all interviews with members of the A.F.P. will be confidential.
However, there's still a possibility further evidence will be obtained in public hearings, after the in-camera interviews are completed.
CLUB KEEPING CLOSE EYE ON SWANS THIS WEEK
Sydney Swans officials are hoping the groundswell of interest in the team since it advanced to the A-F-L Grand final, won't have any effect on its performance next Saturday.
Swans football manager Rob Snowden says Club officials will be working to ensure players are not over committed by outside engagements this week.
All players escaped unscathed in their one-point victory over Essendon last Saturday, and are expected to be at full strength for the Grand Final.
Match hero, Tony Lockett pulled up sore after the game but Snowden says he'll be fit for Saturday's M-C-G clash.
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY AT TEN YEAR PEAK
A new survey has found housing affordability in Australia is at its highest level in ten years... mainly due to steady wages growth, and falling interest rates.
The Wespac Bank's 1996 spring housing report shows the relationship between house prices and wages is back where it was ten years ago, with buying conditions continuing to improve.
Westpac's general manager of economics, Bill Evans, says it's clear that its easier to afford a house now, than at any time in the last decade.
Westpac is also forecasting an improvement in residential construction, with New South Wales and Victoria in the best positions for recovery.
The bank says Western Australia's prospects continue to depend on the strength of the states mining sector.
NSW FORESTRY DECISION TODAY
New South Wales Land and Water Conservation Minister Kim Yeadon says there's been unprecedented community input in the lead-up to today's Cabinet decision on forests.
Green groups have warned the Government its conservation credentials are on the line, while timber unions have warned of mass protests if jobs are not protected.
Mr Yeadon says there've been 20-thousand submissions from workers, conservationists and mill owners, plus face-to-face sessions with all key interest groups.
The Cabinet is expected to endorse the Government's forestry policy, and the minister says it'll be a balanced decision.
